feed.topic: AI agents · tool use and function calling
feed.summary: We present Salesforce Koa, an enterprise language model built by post-training the open-weight Nemotron-3-Super-120B foundation model with reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
feed.whyRelevant: Composio and Optexity both sit on the boundary between a model and the systems it acts on, which is where these failures are measured.

feed.emailBody:
A paper worth ten minutes — Salesforce Koa: An Enterprise Language Model for Agentic Tool Use (arXiv, 14 September 2026):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15066

We present Salesforce Koa, an enterprise language model built by post-training the open-weight Nemotron-3-Super-120B foundation model with reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

Where does a tool call most often go wrong for you: selection, arguments, or the result coming back in a shape the model misreads?
takeaways: From the abstract: “These results show that specification-driven reinforcement learning is a practical path to specializing open-weight foundation models for enterprise agentic tasks.”

From the abstract: “Salesforce Koa is trained on public and synthetically generated data, with no customer data, to improve tool use and agentic capabilities while preserving strong general-purpose performance.”

From the abstract: “Its distinctive component is a simulation-to-reward pipeline that expands workflow specifications into persona-conditioned multi-turn tasks with task-resolution rewards grounded in successful tool use for data-dependent requests.”
feed.discussionQuestion: Where does a tool call most often go wrong for you: selection, arguments, or the result coming back in a shape the model misreads?

Table extraction from texts is an important task for information systems, and recent approaches that prompt large language models (LLMs) with instructions have drawn great attention for their strong performance.

feed.summary: Per-layer differential privacy (DP) clipping improves gradient fidelity in federated learning by allocating per-matrix clipping budgets proportional to parameter count.
feed.whyRelevant: Both companies sell privacy assurances, so the gap between formal guarantees and what is deployable matters commercially.

feed.emailSubject: Worth a read: Component-Aware Differential Privacy for Federated Mult…
feed.emailBody:
A paper worth ten minutes — Component-Aware Differential Privacy for Federated Multilingual Speech-LLMs (arXiv, 10 September 2026):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11762

Per-layer differential privacy (DP) clipping improves gradient fidelity in federated learning by allocating per-matrix clipping budgets proportional to parameter count.

Do buyers ask for a formal guarantee, or for evidence that nothing leaked?
takeaways: From the abstract: “We show that this recipe breaks for speech large language models (speech-LLMs), when the acoustic encoder and the language decoder differ by an order of magnitude in update norm.”

From the abstract: “At architecture-calibrated $α$, our method recovers WER utility compared to flat DP, while granting the encoder $4.47{\times}$ tighter per-component noise protection against speaker voice-based gradient-inversion attacks at only $+2.6\%$ LLM noise overhead.”
From the abstract: “Single-pool per-layer methods suffer \emph{cross-component budget collapse}, dragging word error rate (WER) far from flat global clipping or collapsing training entirely.”
feed.discussionQuestion: Do buyers ask for a formal guarantee, or for evidence that nothing leaked?

feed.title: RevenueHero published inbound funnel benchmarks from a million form submissions
feed.summary: RevenueHero co-founder Charanyan publishes qualified-to-booked benchmarks drawn from over one million B2B SaaS inbound form submissions across its customer base, segmented by company size.
feed.whyRelevant: A portfolio founder published a benchmark other portfolio founders can measure themselves against this week. It gives a specific number to compare rather than general advice.
feed.engagementMove: Send the 62% median as a yardstick, ask for their number, and offer a working session with the RevenueHero founders.
feed.emailSubject: A 62% benchmark to measure your inbound against
feed.emailBody:
RevenueHero published inbound benchmarks from more than a million B2B form submissions:
https://www.revenuehero.io/blog/demo-request-to-booked-conversion-rate-benchmarks-in-2026

The median qualified-to-booked rate is 62%, and booking probability falls from roughly 80% in the first minute to about 40% by the next business day. Worth knowing where you sit — happy to set up a conversation with their team.
takeaways: The baseline: “The median qualified-to-booked rate across all customers is 62%.” and “The top 10% hit 78% or higher.”
By segment: “SMB-focused companies convert at 63.2% with a 21.8% disqualification rate.”
Speed is the lever: “The probability of booking a meeting drops from roughly 80% in the first minute to around 40% by the next business day.”
feed.discussionQuestion: What share of your qualified inbound actually converts into a booked meeting, and how quickly?

Large language models (LLMs) are used to simulate human participants in psychological research.

feed.title: What AI answers say about software pricing
feed.publisher: Profound · Kyle Poyar and Nikolas Laskaris
feed.summary: The authors tested 7,600 pricing responses across six AI engines and Cloud 100 companies, finding that company pricing pages often were not the primary cited source.
feed.whyRelevant: For RevenueHero, buyers may arrive at the demo with a preformed pricing view. For Spendflo, it is a prompt to examine how buyers research and compare vendors. Vendor-authored, time-bounded research.
feed.emailSubject: What buyers may believe before they request a demo
feed.emailBody:
This pricing study from Kyle Poyar and Profound is worth a look:
https://www.tryprofound.com/blog/what-ai-agents-really-think-about-your-pricing

They tested AI-generated pricing answers and found that official pricing pages often were not the main source. A practical experiment would be to audit a handful of common buyer questions against the actual offer.

Are pricing misunderstandings showing up earlier in your funnel, or only once a sales conversation begins?
takeaways: A visible pricing page may still hide its details from crawlers through rendering or interaction requirements.
The authors recommend consistent pricing, billing explanations and FAQs; their observed citation patterns are time-bounded.
feed.discussionQuestion: Which buyer pricing question produces an answer that differs from the current offer, and which source caused the mismatch?

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: RevenueHero's marketing co-founder works on B2B acquisition and revenue operations.
recipientAngles.angle: Audit the pricing expectations buyers bring to a demo.
recipientAngles.emailSubject: A five-question audit before the demo request
recipientAngles.emailBody:
Profound's pricing study suggests a small RevenueHero marketing exercise: ask five real buyer questions in an AI search tool, then compare each answer with the current offer. Record the wrong claim, its source and the page that should answer it. Which question would you start with?

https://www.tryprofound.com/blog/what-ai-agents-really-think-about-your-pricing

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: Spendflo's CPO works on SaaS purchasing and vendor comparisons.
recipientAngles.angle: Separate discovered pricing claims from verified procurement inputs.
recipientAngles.emailSubject: Keeping AI-discovered pricing separate from a quote
recipientAngles.emailBody:
This Profound study prompted a Spendflo workflow idea: show a discovered vendor price beside its source, date, unit and verification status before it enters a comparison. Which assumption would you insist on confirming with the vendor before using that number in a buying recommendation?

https://www.tryprofound.com/blog/what-ai-agents-really-think-about-your-pricing

feed.title: Fewer than one in ten practices report faster prior authorization in 2026
feed.summary: An MGMA Stat poll of 178 medical group leaders, fielded 1 September 2026, finds prior-authorization turnaround has not improved despite new federal requirements on payer decision times.
feed.whyRelevant: This is third-party, recent, quotable buyer-side evidence for healthcare founders to use in their own sales conversations, rather than something they need to tell us about their market.
feed.engagementMove: Hand over as a dated stat pack for their outreach and deck, and ask which workflow their customers name first.
feed.emailSubject: Fresh prior-auth burden data you can quote
feed.emailBody:
MGMA polled 178 medical group leaders on 1 September:
https://www.mgma.com/mgma-stat/fewer-than-1-in-10-see-prior-auth-turnarounds-faster

44% say prior-authorization turnaround got slower this year and only 7% say faster, with 61% of practices touching seven or more payer portals a week. Recent and quotable for your own conversations.
takeaways: The headline finding: “44% of medical group leaders said payer prior authorization turnaround became slower in 2026 compared with 2025. Another 40% said turnaround is about the same, while 7% reported faster turnaround.”
The workflow detail that matters for product: “61% of practices had staff accessing seven or more payer portals each week.”
The poll is dated and sized: fielded 1 September 2026 with 178 applicable responses.
feed.discussionQuestion: Which part of the payer workflow do your customers complain about first — the wait, or the number of portals?

A paper worth ten minutes — Cloud and On-Premises Deployment of Uzbek Legal RAG via Targeted Retriever Fine-Tuning (arXiv, 29 August 2026):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29284

Deploying large language models for legal question answering raises challenges that general-purpose leaderboards do not capture, particularly for low-resource languages and under hard operational constraints.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08362

Recent Text-To-Speech (TTS) systems have achieved strong naturalness and zero-shot voice cloning performance, but fine-grained control of expressive speech at the word or phoneme level remains challenging.

How much of a good voice interaction is recognition quality versus knowing when to stop talking?
takeaways: From the abstract: “We propose CtrlSpeech, a controllable, expressive TTS framework with coarse-to-fine control.”

From the abstract: “Experimental results show that CtrlSpeech achieves competitive zero-shot TTS performance and improves controllability over expressive attributes, demonstrating its effectiveness for flexible and practical expressive speech synthesis.”

From the abstract: “Built on the DiTAR architecture, CtrlSpeech combines global speaker conditioning with phone-aligned pitch, loudness, and duration signals, enabling localized prosodic control while preserving the target speaker's timbre.”

feed.title: CFOs are using AI widely but only 43% are confident in their governance
feed.topic: Finance buyers · AI adoption, governance and cost transparency
feed.summary: Deloitte’s Q2 2026 CFO Signals survey of 200 CFOs at North American organizations with at least $1 billion in revenue finds broad AI use alongside limited confidence in governance and a clear top concern about cost.
feed.whyRelevant: For anyone selling into the finance organization, this names the objection before it is raised: cost uncertainty, not capability, is what CFOs worry about most.
feed.engagementMove: Send to founders selling into finance and offer to pressure-test how their pricing answers the cost-uncertainty objection.
feed.emailSubject: What CFOs actually worry about when buying AI
feed.emailBody:
Deloitte surveyed 200 CFOs at companies with $1B+ revenue:
https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/topics/business-strategy-growth/2q-2026-cfo-signals-survey.html

Their top internal concern about AI is cost uncertainty or lack of transparency, not capability, and only 43% feel confident in their AI governance. Useful framing if the finance org is in your buying group.
takeaways: Governance confidence is thin: “While 43% say they feel confident, more than half (53.5%) feel only somewhat confident.”
The number one internal concern is cost: “46% of respondents say their biggest internal concern about their organization's use of AI is cost uncertainty or lack of transparency—the No.1 response.”
Finance functions are already using it: “44% of respondents are using AI for financial planning and budgeting.”
feed.discussionQuestion: Does your pricing make the cost predictable enough for a CFO to approve without a contingency?

Table extraction from business documents relies on a cascaded pipeline where Table Detection (TD) first localizes tables and Table Structure Recognition (TSR) then recovers their internal layout.

feed.title: Enterprise buyers are deploying agents but cannot measure the return
feed.topic: Enterprise buying · agent adoption and ROI
feed.summary: Battery Ventures surveyed 100 senior technology leaders representing more than $66 billion in annual technology spend, finding agentic deployment rising sharply while ROI measurement remains largely unsolved.
feed.whyRelevant: The 94% figure is the most useful number here: it says buyers cannot measure value on their own, so the vendor that supplies the measurement wins the renewal. That is a sales-strategy prompt, not sector news.
feed.engagementMove: Send as buyer-side evidence and offer to review the ROI slide in their enterprise deck.
feed.emailSubject: 94% of enterprise buyers have no way to measure AI ROI
feed.emailBody:
Battery surveyed 100 senior technology leaders representing more than $66 billion in annual tech spend:
https://www.battery.com/blog/survey-says-agentic-ai-penetrates-the-enterprise-but-some-roi-questions-remain/

49% are actively deploying agents and 81% plan to increase spend, but 94% have no consistent framework for evaluating AI ROI. That last number seems like the opening — whoever supplies the measurement owns the renewal conversation.
takeaways: Adoption is moving fast: “49% of respondents said they're actively deploying agentic AI, up from 33% six months ago.”
Budget is following: “An impressive 81% plan to increase overall tech spending over the next 12 months, up from 65% in December 2025.”
The opening for vendors: “A very sizable 94% of respondents said their organizations lacked a consistent, enterprise-wide framework for evaluating AI's ROI.”
feed.discussionQuestion: If 94% of buyers have no ROI framework, whose numbers does your champion use at renewal?

https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22249

In recent years, weight quantization that encodes the learnable parameters of large language models in an $n$-bit format has garnered significant attention due to its potential for model compression and inference acceleration.

Which would move your product more: half the latency, or half the cost?
takeaways: From the abstract: “Many practical techniques have been developed; however, the theoretical understanding of many aspects, especially the approximation and degradation of expressive power as the number of quantization bits decreases, remains unclear.”

feed.summary: Coding agents have become a major mode of software engineering, but the benchmarks we use to compare them were designed in a pre-agent era: they collapse model, harness, and environment into a single end-to-end score, typically computed against one reference solution, with no component-level signal for iteration.
feed.whyRelevant: Emergent and Rocket build with agents at repository scale, and Hivel measures what engineering teams produce, so task-completion evidence is relevant to all three.

feed.emailBody:
A paper worth ten minutes — Position: Coding Benchmarks Are Misaligned with Agentic Software Engineering (arXiv, 16 June 2026):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17799

Coding agents have become a major mode of software engineering, but the benchmarks we use to compare them were designed in a pre-agent era: they collapse model, harness, and environment into a single end-to-end score, typically computed against one reference solution, with no component-level signal for iteration.

At repository scale, is the limiting factor the model, the context it gets, or the verification loop?
takeaways: From the abstract: “A coding agent in practice is not a model: it is a system harness -- a composite of models, harnesses, contexts, environments, and feedback signals, any one of which can move the benchmark score by margins comparable to those between adjacent model generations.”

From the abstract: “We discuss three symptoms: (i) benchmark scores conflate the model with the rest of the harness; (ii) grading against a single reference solution penalises equally valid alternatives; and (iii) the absence of signal at the level of individual harness components makes the end-to-end system score d…”
From the abstract: “We argue that current coding benchmarks are misaligned with agentic software engineering.”

feed.title: Segment choice at $10k MRR still predicts the business three years later
feed.topic: Company building · customer segment and retention
feed.summary: Using ChartMogul data on 1,043 SaaS and AI companies that reached $10k MRR by May 2023 and were still operating in May 2026, Poyar shows that the customer segment a company serves early tends to persist, and that segment shapes growth.
feed.whyRelevant: A dated, sourced answer to a decision most early founders make implicitly. It is most useful before a company has locked in its segment, which is exactly where several portfolio companies sit.
feed.engagementMove: Send to pre-scale founders with one question about which segment they are actually converting, not which one they target.
feed.emailSubject: The segment you pick early tends to stick
feed.emailBody:
Kyle Poyar looked at 1,043 companies from $10k MRR onward using ChartMogul data:
https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/startups-become-what-they-hunt

The finding that stayed with me is that 70% kept the same target customer three years later. Worth asking whether the segment converting today is the one you actually want.
takeaways: Segment choice is sticky: “When I mapped where companies started versus where they ended up, animal migrations turned out to be rare. 70% kept the same target customer.”
Mid-market compounds: “Companies that started as deer hunters and stayed there are growing revenue at an average of 22% year-over-year.”
Companies are grouped by average revenue per account: mouse under $30/month, rabbit $30–299, deer $300–2,999, elephant $3,000+.
feed.discussionQuestion: Is the segment you are winning today the segment you want to be serving in three years?

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: Nex is early enough that its CRM segment is still being decided by which deals close.
recipientAngles.angle: Discuss whether the converting segment matches the intended one.
recipientAngles.emailSubject: Which segment is actually converting for Nex?
recipientAngles.emailBody:
This analysis of 1,043 companies found that 70% kept the same target customer three years after reaching $10k MRR:
https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/startups-become-what-they-hunt

The uncomfortable version of the question for any early CRM: is the segment closing today the one you chose, or the one that happened to say yes first?

Since you are still working with design partners, this feels like the moment the choice is actually made. Are your partners representative of the segment you want, or the one that was easiest to recruit?

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: Zipy serves both smaller teams and mid-market engineering organizations.

recipientAngles.emailBody:
This ChartMogul-based analysis found companies that stayed in the mid-market band grew about 22% year-over-year:
https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/startups-become-what-they-hunt

Zipy spans a range of account sizes. Is there a deliberate reason to keep the span wide, or would concentrating change what you build next?

A paper worth ten minutes — RAGe: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation Framework (arXiv, 23 May 2026):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27445

Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) applications, particularly those relying on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), remains challenging due to high computational demands, outdated knowledge bases, and the need to manually select optimal pipeline components.

When a grounded answer is wrong, can you tell whether retrieval or generation failed?

A paper worth ten minutes — Probabilistic-bit Guided CDCL for SAT Solving using Ising Consensus Assumptions (arXiv, 5 May 2026):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04033

Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solvers are widely used in hardware verification, cryptanalysis, automatic test-pattern generation, and side-channel reasoning workflows.

Does an AI-written testbench reduce verification time, or move the review burden?
takeaways: From the abstract: “Modern conflict-driven clause-learning (CDCL) solvers are highly effective, but satisfiable instances may still require substantial conflict analysis and Boolean propagation before identifying productive regions of the search space.”

From the abstract: “This paper studies a hybrid SAT-solving framework in which a probabilistic-bit (p-bit) Ising sampler proposes high-agreement literals that are passed to CDCL as temporary assumptions.”

From the abstract: “The goal is not to replace CDCL, but to evaluate whether stochastic low-violation samples can reduce CDCL internal search effort while retaining correctness through CDCL fallback.”
feed.discussionQuestion: Does an AI-written testbench reduce verification time, or move the review burden?

feed.emailBody:
A paper worth ten minutes — Statistically-Lossless Quantization of Large Language Models (arXiv, 4 May 2026):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02404

Model quantization has become essential for efficient large language model deployment, yet existing approaches present clear trade-offs: methods such as GPTQ and AWQ achieve practical compression but are lossy, while lossless techniques preserve fidelity but lack inference acceleration.

Which would move your product more: half the latency, or half the cost?
takeaways: From the abstract: “First, task-lossless compression preserves zero-shot benchmark accuracy within natural sampling variance and is achievable at aggressive bitwidths.”

From the abstract: “Third, we prove a gamma-squared variance law showing that symmetric quantization inflates noise variance by gamma^2 relative to asymmetric quantization, making asymmetric quantization a prerequisite for distribution-lossless fidelity but not for task-level preservation.”
From the abstract: “This paper explores the middle ground of statistically-lossless compression, examining three complementary aspects of what losslessness means for quantized LLMs.”

A paper worth ten minutes — EdgeSpike: Spiking Neural Networks for Low-Power Autonomous Sensing in Edge IoT Architectures (arXiv, 29 April 2026):

We propose EdgeSpike, a co-designed spiking neural network (SNN) framework for autonomous low-power sensing in edge Internet of Things (IoT) architectures.

What would have to be true before customers wanted inference on the device rather than in your cloud?
takeaways: From the abstract: “EdgeSpike achieves a mean classification accuracy of 91.4%, within 1.2 percentage points (pp) of strong INT8 convolutional neural network (CNN) baselines (mean 92.6%), while reducing energy per inference by 18x to 47x on neuromorphic hardware (mean 31x) and by 4.6x to 7.9x on Cortex-M (mean 6.1x).”

From the abstract: “EdgeSpike will be released as open source with reproducible training pipelines, hardware-portable runtimes, and benchmark suites.”

https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22534

Feature engineering for Electronic Health Records (EHR) is complicated by irregular observation intervals, variable measurement frequencies, and structural sparsity inherent to clinical time series.

Which part of the administrative workflow is actually safe to complete without a human in the loop?
takeaways: From the abstract: “We present \textbf{FeatEHR-LLM}, a framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate clinically meaningful tabular features from irregularly sampled EHR time series.”

A paper worth ten minutes — MemBoost: A Memory-Boosted Framework for Cost-Aware LLM Inference (arXiv, 27 March 2026):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26557

Large Language Models (LLMs) deliver strong performance but incur high inference cost in real-world services, especially under workloads with repeated or near-duplicate queries across users and sessions.

Do your customers yet treat inference as a line item they manage, or as part of the software price?
takeaways: From the abstract: “In this work, we propose MemBoost, a memory-boosted LLM serving framework that enables a lightweight model to reuse previously generated answers and retrieve relevant supporting information for cheap inference, while selectively escalating difficult or uncertain queries to a stronger model.”

From the abstract: “Unlike standard retrieval-augmented generation, which primarily grounds a single response, MemBoost is designed for interactive settings by supporting answer reuse, continual memory growth, and cost-aware routing.”

From the abstract: “Experiments across multiple models under simulated workloads show that MemBoost substantially reduces expensive large-model invocations and overall inference cost, while maintaining high answer quality comparable to the strong model baseline.”

Engineers describe some creation-time savings moving into review and verification. My takeaway is to look at the full delivery path, including rework and stability, when judging the impact of AI tools.

A paper worth ten minutes — Counterfactual Simulation Training for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness (arXiv, 24 February 2026):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20710

Inspecting Chain-of-Thought reasoning is among the most common means of understanding why an LLM produced its output.

If the explanation is wrong but the answer is right, does that matter for your users?
takeaways: From the abstract: “In this paper, we introduce a training method called Counterfactual Simulation Training (CST), which aims to improve CoT faithfulness by rewarding CoTs that enable a simulator to accurately predict a model's outputs over counterfactual inputs.”

feed.title: FinOps expands from cloud bills into SaaS and AI value
feed.summary: The 2026 survey shows FinOps teams broadening into SaaS and AI, with demand for granular cost visibility, forecasting and business-value attribution.

feed.emailSubject: An interesting shift in who owns SaaS and AI spend
feed.emailBody:
The State of FinOps 2026 report has a useful shift in buying context:
https://data.finops.org/

FinOps is increasingly covering SaaS and AI alongside cloud infrastructure. My takeaway is that buyers may need a shared view of commitments, usage and business value, beyond a renewal-saving number.

Are your conversations moving toward variable AI consumption and attribution, or is the immediate need still visibility into existing contracts?
takeaways: Respondents want cost estimates before deployment and more granular AI cost data.
Allocation, forecasting and planning remain foundational as FinOps extends beyond cloud infrastructure.
feed.discussionQuestion: Before a variable-use software commitment, can the buyer name its consumption assumptions, budget owner and response if usage exceeds the estimate?

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: Spendflo's CPO works on procurement and SaaS-spend products.
recipientAngles.angle: Bring usage scenarios into purchasing and renewal decisions.
recipientAngles.emailSubject: A pre-purchase worksheet for variable AI spend
recipientAngles.emailBody:
The FinOps survey suggests a Spendflo procurement worksheet: committed spend, expected usage range, overage terms and the owner of each assumption. I'd test it on one AI-software purchase before negotiating the discount. Which missing input is most likely to change the purchase decision?

https://data.finops.org/

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: Togai's co-founder has public usage-billing and metering expertise; the company was acquired by Zuora.
recipientAngles.angle: Discuss billing explainability from metering experience, without assuming a current employer.

recipientAngles.emailBody:
Given your work on Togai, the FinOps survey raised a billing question I'd value your view on: what should a customer receive to reconcile one usage charge without a support ticket? My starting list would be the billable event, unit, rate and treatment of retries. What would you add?

feed.title: A first-hand account of redesigning hiring assessments for AI
feed.summary: Anthropic's performance-engineering team explains three versions of its take-home assessment as improving models made earlier tests less discriminating.
feed.whyRelevant: A concrete employer case for Kula and Hunar when discussing evidence of candidate ability. It concerns one specialist engineering role and should not be generalized to all hiring.
feed.emailSubject: A concrete hiring-assessment problem to compare notes on
feed.emailBody:
This first-hand account from Anthropic is a useful prompt for hiring teams:
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/AI-resistant-technical-evaluations

They kept redesigning a take-home as models caught up. The broader question it raises for me is what evidence an assessment captures about the candidate's judgment, especially when AI help is permitted.

Are your customers changing the assessment itself, or mainly asking how to interpret AI-assisted submissions?
takeaways: Anthropic explicitly allowed AI for this specialist assessment; that exception was not its general take-home policy.
Later versions traded some job realism for unfamiliar problems that better separated candidates from models.
feed.discussionQuestion: What candidate judgment can a hiring team observe separately from the finished AI-assisted submission?

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: Kula's CTO combines recruiting technology with engineering hiring context.
recipientAngles.angle: Help employers state what their assessments actually measure.
recipientAngles.emailSubject: What remains observable in an AI-assisted assessment?
recipientAngles.emailBody:
Anthropic's assessment story suggests a useful Kula customer question: what evidence does the rubric capture beyond a completed answer? I'd separate the result, the candidate's verification steps and their explanation of tradeoffs. Would a hiring team be able to defend its decision from that record?

https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/AI-resistant-technical-evaluations

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: Emergent's CTO works on AI coding and agent evaluation.

recipientAngles.emailBody:
This Anthropic hiring case seems relevant to an AI-coding team. A possible interview exercise: ask a candidate to inspect an agent-produced change, choose what to verify, and explain one rejected shortcut. recipientAngles.emailBody:

For one frontline role, could a supervisor distinguish information verified in a screening conversation from ability that needs a practical check? Which distinction should the product make explicit?

feed.title: LinkedIn's hiring research: more applicants, harder matching
feed.summary: LinkedIn reports that US applicants per open role doubled since spring 2022, while surveyed recruiters describe difficulty finding qualified talent and growing interest in AI screening.
feed.whyRelevant: This frames a useful product discussion about qualification quality versus application volume for Kula and Hunar. It is LinkedIn's own research, with US-specific applicant data.
feed.emailSubject: More applicants, but harder matching
feed.emailBody:
LinkedIn's January research puts applicant growth and recruiter frustration side by side:
https://news.linkedin.com/2026/LinkedIn-Research-Talent-2026

The useful tension is that more applicants do not necessarily make the right candidate easier to find. It suggests measuring the quality of the shortlist, not just time saved in screening.

Recruiters' plans to expand AI screening are stated intentions, not demonstrated hiring outcomes.

feed.title: APTA's survey of administrative burden in physical therapy
feed.summary: APTA's survey connects payer administration with staffing burden, delayed authorization and reported treatment abandonment. It captures respondents' experiences, not a causal trial.
feed.whyRelevant: Directly relevant to SPRY's physical-therapy practice workflows. An evergreen source for selecting measurable administrative outcomes that matter to clinic operators.
feed.emailSubject: A clinic-operator lens on administrative ROI
feed.emailBody:
This APTA report from November is still a useful clinic-operator reference:
https://www.apta.org/advocacy/issues/administrative-burden/report

It links administrative burden with staffing needs and delays in getting patients into treatment. My takeaway for a workflow product is to connect hours saved to a concrete operational result, such as fewer pending authorizations or less time until treatment starts.

Which of those outcomes is easiest for a clinic to measure and act on today?
takeaways: Thirty percent of surveyed respondents reported waiting one to two weeks for authorization.
Respondents also reported added staffing and payer-network exits; these are survey experiences, not measured causal effects.
feed.discussionQuestion: Can a clinic connect authorization delays to deferred appointments and staff effort using records it already keeps?

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: SPRY's co-founder focuses on healthcare operations and practice management.
recipientAngles.angle: Turn a broad administrative-burden claim into a manageable clinic queue.
recipientAngles.emailSubject: A practical authorization queue for clinic operators
recipientAngles.emailBody:
APTA's survey suggests an operating exercise for SPRY: take a week's pending authorizations and record payer, days waiting, next action and the appointment affected. Would a clinic manager get more value from that queue than a total-hours-saved figure? Which field could staff reliably maintain without extra work?

https://www.apta.org/advocacy/issues/administrative-burden/report

recipientAngles.whyThisPerson: SPRY's CEO works across rehabilitation workflows and revenue cycle.
recipientAngles.angle: Measure clinic value through care access and capacity as well as efficiency.
recipientAngles.emailSubject: Showing administrative ROI in clinic terms
recipientAngles.emailBody:
The APTA findings prompted a possible SPRY pilot scorecard: staff time spent chasing authorization, days until the first visit, and appointments postponed while waiting. I'd establish the baseline with the clinic before choosing a target. Which measure best captures value without claiming that software alone changes clinical outcomes?
